_meta.source: ACAPS Risk Radar export (data/risk-radar-export.csv), used under ACAPS terms of use
_meta.note: Real ACAPS triggers for all 33 risks in risks.json. Completion rates and histories are as exported; source URLs are cleaned of the trailing escape character.

items.title: Lethal militant attack in a major Pakistani urban centre.
items.description: A confirmed TTP attack targeting Pakistani security forces or government installations in cities such as Karachi, Peshawar, or Islamabad is likely to trigger further Pakistani airstrikes or ground operations in Afghan border provinces. Historically, such events have served as the primary political trigger for Pakistani retaliatory airstrikes and ground operations in Afghan border provinces like Paktia and Paktika. The 28 June attack was carried out by Pakistan, according to Pakistani authorities, in retaliation for an alleged TTP attack on security personnel in Karachi days earlier.

items.title: Cross-border hostilities
items.description: Clashes between army forces in bordering areas and the closure of borders will limit movement, constrain access of humanitarian aid, interrupt livelihoods and trade between communities. In past border closures food security and livelihoods have been significantly impacted.

items.title: Expanded ITA disarmament order or offensive in the north of Afghanistan:
items.description: Further efforts by the ITA to disarm opposition groups and consolidate control over local commanders could trigger armed resistance and renewed clashes in Badakhshan, particularly in areas where armed groups retain influence.
items.resolutionCriterion: depending on the number of armed groups active and in which areas.

items.title: Armed group offensives could restrict and attacks in districts centres:
items.description: Renewed attacks or attempts by armed groups to seize district centres could disrupt movement, displace civilians, and restrict humanitarian access to affected communities.
items.resolutionCriterion: the number of renewed attacks or attempts.

items.title: Cross border conflicts.
items.description: Cross border interest because of proximity with China, and cross border conflicts with Pakistan, could increase the presence of armed actors and affect local communities. Badakhshan is considered a key route for drug trafficking because of its geography and long border with Tajikistan.
items.resolutionCriterion: number of attacks related to cross border conflict.

items.title: Expansion of cross-border attacks and insecurity
items.description: Additional drone strikes, shelling, or armed incursions near the Chad–Sudan border, particularly around Adré, Tina, and other eastern border localities, increase civilian casualties, trigger further displacement into Chad, and constrain humanitarian operations in already fragile border areas. Continued insecurity may also disrupt cross-border trade and movement routes relied upon by refugees and host communities
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% completion would be reached if cross-border attacks become sustained and recurrent, affecting multiple border localities in eastern Chad and causing significant civilian casualties, displacement, or humanitarian access disruptions.

items.title: Attacks on strategic infrastructure in Chad
items.description: Threats by Sudanese actors against Chadian airports, border facilities, military positions, or transport infrastructure may materialise into direct attacks on strategic assets in eastern Chad. Any strike against airports such as Amdjarass, military installations, or critical transport corridors would increase the risk of direct confrontation between Chad and Sudanese armed actors, disrupt humanitarian and commercial operations, and further destabilise border regions
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% completion would be reached if attacks directly target strategic infrastructure in Chad, including airports, military facilities, border posts, or major transport corridors, causing significant disruption to civilian, humanitarian, or commercial activities.

items.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
items.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian territory.
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% completion would be reached if armed groups, militias, or proxy actors operating across the Chad–Sudan border become actively involved in cross-border hostilities, resulting in sustained violence, retaliatory attacks, or territorial insecurity in eastern Chad.

items.title: Retaliatory violence following the killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki
items.description: The reported killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki by US and Nigerian forces on 15 May 2026 could trigger retaliatory attacks by ISWAP, while intensifying competition with JAS/Boko Haram for territorial influence and operational relevance. Escalating attacks against military positions, civilians, and strategic infrastructure—particularly in Borno State—could increase displacement and humanitarian needs, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may generate spillover effects into Niger’s Diffa region, Cameroon’s Far North, and Chad’s Lac Province.
items.resolutionCriterion: Increased retaliatory attacks by ISWAP and/or JAS/Boko Haram following the killing of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, resulting in sustained increases in attacks against military positions and civilians in Borno with spillover into neighbouring countries.

items.title: Expansion of military counteroffensives and emergency security measures
items.description: Nigerian and regional security forces may intensify military operations, including cross-border operations and emergency security measures, in response to rising insurgent activity. Expanded military deployments, movement restrictions, and operations around Lake Chad and border areas could increase civilian displacement, disrupt livelihoods, and further constrain humanitarian access, particularly if armed groups respond with additional attacks or shift operations across borders
items.resolutionCriterion: Expansion of Nigerian and regional military operations, including cross-border operations and movement restrictions, leading to increased civilian displacement and humanitarian access constraints across the Lake Chad Basin.

items.title: Launch of the 90-Day Security Crackdown
items.description: The incoming government’s planned military offensive against NSAGs from 7 August, including bombing campaigns against armed group camps, aerial coca fumigation, deployment of Joint Task Forces to Cauca, Chocó, and Nariño, and increased defence investment, is expected to provoke armed group retaliation against security forces and civilians perceived to be cooperating with the State.

items.title: NSAG consolidation and territorial expansion
items.description: The significant strengthening of NSAGs since 2022, including a reported increase in membership, territorial expansion, adoption of new tactics, and increased reliance on illicit economies such as coca cultivation and illegal mining, increases the likelihood that armed groups will seek to consolidate control over contested territories and demonstrate operational capacity ahead of and during the anticipated offensive.

items.title: Formal termination of peace negotiations
items.description: A decision by the incoming government to end the outgoing administration’s “Total Peace” talks with NSAGs would remove an important mechanism for dialogue and de-escalation. The breakdown of ELN talks preceding the escalation of fighting in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) in January 2025 illustrates how quickly violence and displacement can increase following the collapse of negotiations.

items.title: Bureaucratic cuts and public sector purges
items.description: Implementation of the pledged 40% reduction in the state apparatus and removal of officials linked to the outgoing administration could trigger sustained protest mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the security risk through potential clashes with security forces and increased protection concerns.

items.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia's key Meher-producing areas
items.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing by 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with precipitation deficits likely in the northeastern and central areas, where there is at least a 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more. This combination of reduced rainfall and above average temperatures during the critical Kiremt season is expected to suppress Meher crop yields, reduce agricultural labour demand, and accelerate pasture and water scarcity in pastoral areas.

items.title: Strengthening El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December season in lowland and riverine areas of Ethiopia
items.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during the October–December season across eastern East Africa. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, there is an increased likelihood of flooding across flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia, especially the Somali Region. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa.

items.title: Sustained increase in hotspots and peatland fires
items.description: A continued rise in hotspots and burned area across West and Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra, Riau, and Jambi, particularly where fires spread into deep peat, would indicate that suppression operations are not containing the fire season. Fires persisting underground or reigniting after initial suppression would increase the likelihood of prolonged smoke exposure.

items.title: Prolonged dry conditions and peak El Nino
items.description: Below-average rainfall, extreme heat, declining water availability ahead of El Nino peak towards the end of 2026 could dry vegetation and peat further. This would allow fires to spread more rapidly and simultaneously across several provinces, stretching firefighting capacity.

items.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September rainfall across western and northern Kenya
items.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing during May–July 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal JJAS rainfall across western and northern Kenya — where the unimodal long rains season in fact extends into August/September and has already tracked below average in April and early May — alongside above-normal temperatures. This combination is expected to reduce soil moisture during the critical grain-filling and maturation stages of long rains crops in the North Rift and western Kenya, directly threatening the October–November harvest. Pastoral areas across the ASALs are likely to experience accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability, compounding already fragile livestock recovery.

items.title: El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December short rains season in eastern and coastal Kenya
items.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during Kenya's October–December short rains season, particularly across eastern and coastal areas. During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comparable pattern of enhanced short rains is likely. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Should this materialise, flooding would damage infrastructure and cropland in areas already weakened by successive climate shocks, further compounding humanitarian needs heading into early 2027.

items.title: Rainfall deficits and above average precipitation affecting agricultural production
items.description: Dry conditions are likely to lead to reduced soil moisture, crop failure, and declining pasture availability, which in turn limit household food production and income from agriculture. This reduces food availability at the household level and increases reliance on markets at a time of constrained purchasing power.

items.title: Expansion of coordinated JNIM–FLA operations
items.description: Coordinated attacks by JNIM and the FLA against military bases, urban centres, and strategic infrastructure may continue or expand into additional regions, increasing territorial contestation and exposing civilians to heightened insecurity. Although likely tactical and temporary, continued operational coordination between both actors could allow simultaneous attacks across multiple regions and increase pressure on Malian forces. Sustained cooperation may also increase pressure on transport corridors and urban areas, particularly around central and northern Mali, while complicating military operations and humanitarian access. Further attacks on strategic towns or military positions could increase insecurity in areas previously considered comparatively more stable.
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% completion would be reached if coordinated JNIM–FLA operations expand beyond current areas of activity and result in sustained attacks against additional strategic urban centres, transport corridors, or military installations across northern and central Mali.

items.title: Intensification of military operations and retaliatory violence
items.description: In response to the coordinated attacks, Malian forces and allied armed actors may increase military operations, aerial strikes, and security measures in contested areas. Expanded military deployments around strategic towns, transport corridors, and urban centres may increase movement restrictions and insecurity for civilians. Escalating confrontations and the militarisation of strategic urban centres and transport routes may increase protection risks for civilians, including displacement, restrictions on movement, and disruptions to humanitarian operations and access to essential services. Communities perceived as supporting rival armed actors may also face heightened risks of reprisals, arbitrary restrictions, or violence by conflict parties.
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% completion would be reached if expanded military operations and retaliatory violence result in sustained movement restrictions, significant civilian displacement, widespread protection incidents, or major disruptions to humanitarian access and essential services in conflict-affected areas.

items.title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
items.description: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers.

items.title: Above-average rainfall in northern provinces
items.description: El Niño conditions can enhance moisture inflow in parts of northern Mozambique, leading to above-average and more intense rainfall events. This increases the likelihood of river overflow, flash floods, and waterlogging, especially in low-lying and flood-prone districts. Saturated soils reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff, amplifying flood severity even during short periods of heavy rainfall. Flooding can damage homes, crops, and transport infrastructure, disrupt market access, and increase the risk of population displacement and waterborne diseases, further compounding humanitarian needs.

items.title: Delayed onset and irregular distribution of rains
items.description: El Niño is often associated with a late or erratic start to the rainy season, followed by uneven rainfall patterns throughout the season. In Mozambique, this disrupts the agricultural calendar, delaying planting and reducing the effective growing period for key crops such as maize. Intermittent dry spells during critical crop growth stages can further reduce yields. At the same time, unpredictable rainfall undermines farmers’ decision-making and increases the likelihood of replanting, leading to higher input costs and reduced resilience among households dependent on farming.

items.title: Increased FADM pressure in northern Cabo Delgado
items.description: Continued military operations in Macomia, Muidumbe and surrounding areas could further fragment ISM groups and push fighters towards Quissanga, Meluco, Ancuabe, Chiúre, Montepuez and Niassa. ACLED has documented ISM groups moving south and west following increased state-force pressure in the Catupa area, while subsequent FADM operations also pushed fighters towards Montepuez and the Niassa border.

items.title: July–November hunting season increases the concentration of high-value targets in remote areas:
items.description: The hunting season in Niassa runs through November, bringing increased activity by hunting camps, tourism operators and associated personnel in remote areas of the Niassa Reserve. This creates a seasonal concentration of people, vehicles and other high-value assets in areas with limited security coverage. The 3 September ISM attack on a hunting camp in Marrupa occurred during the current hunting season, indicating that this seasonal activity can create opportunities for NSAG operations in Niassa.

items.title: Changes in the coverage of Rwandan and other external security forces
items.description: A significant reduction, redeployment or change in operational coverage by Rwandan or other external security forces in Cabo Delgado could create additional space for ISM activity and facilitate movement into southern Cabo Delgado and neighbouring provinces. Rwanda was still rotating personnel into Cabo Delgado in July 2026, while Mozambique has continued to describe the Rwandan deployment as an important component of counter-insurgency operations.

items.title: Military reinforcement and establishment of permanent positions in the SEZ
items.description: ·The military reportedly controls Yebyu town and some SEZ compounds, while the wider Nabule area remains contested. The deployment of additional battalions, construction of fortified positions and roadblocks, increased patrols, land clearance, or engineering surveys around Nabule, Wet Chaung, and the deep-sea port site would indicate plans to establish a sustained security perimeter.

items.title: Coordinated resistance offensive against strategic military positions
items.description: A coordinated offensive by KNLA Brigade 4 and allied resistance groups to capture or encircle military positions near the SEZ, Highway 8 or the Myitta–Htee Khee route could trigger a large military counteroffensive involving additional troops and artillery, drone, air or naval support. If the offensive targets positions south of Yebyu or along the border route, the resulting military response could extend into Thayetchaung, the Dawei East Forest and Myitta, increasing civilian casualties and displacement across a wider area.

items.title: Resumption of physical work at the SEZ
items.description: The deployment of technical or construction teams and heavy machinery, renewed land measurement, boundary marking or site clearance, or work on the port, power plant, refinery, LNG facilities or road to Thailand would indicate a shift from political agreements to implementation. If accompanied by increased military deployments or security restrictions, these developments would increase the risk of eviction, land loss and prolonged displacement.

items.title: Increased frequency of direct clashes between JNIM and ISSP in western Niger
items.description: Reports of repeated armed confrontations between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and Tahoua indicate a shift towards sustained inter-group rivalry and territorial contestation. An increase in the frequency, scale, or geographic spread of these clashes would signal a deterioration in the security environment and a higher likelihood of violence against civilians and displacement in affected areas.
items.resolutionCriterion: At least 3–5 reported clashes per month between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and/or Tahoua, or evidence of sustained clashes over a period of 2–3 consecutive weeks.

items.title: Increased targeting of civilians in contested areas
items.description: Reports of killings, abductions, or threats against civilians in areas where JNIM and ISSP are competing for influence, particularly in Tillabéri and Tahoua. Increased violence against civilians may reflect retaliatory dynamics and efforts by both groups to assert territorial control, increasing protection risks and displacement.
items.resolutionCriterion: civilian casualties per month linked to armed group activity in Tillabéri/Tahoua, or a clear increasing trend over 2–3 consecutive months.

items.title: Expansion of inter-group violence into new areas
items.description: Attacks or presence of JNIM or ISSP reported in areas previously less affected, including new localities in Tahoua or neighbouring regions. Geographic expansion would indicate a widening scope of inter-group rivalry and increasing insecurity beyond established hotspots.
items.resolutionCriterion: Confirmed presence or attacks by JNIM and/or ISSP in at least 2–3 new administrative areas (departments or communes) beyond previously affected zones.

items.title: Increase in displacement from western Niger
items.description: Rising displacement flows from Tillabéri and Tahoua linked to insecurity and inter-group clashes. Increased displacement would indicate worsening protection conditions and reduced population resilience in affected areas.
items.resolutionCriterion: An increase of newly displaced people within a short period (1–2 months) linked to insecurity in affected regions.

items.title: Further military dissent, purges, or command disruption:
items.description: Further mutinies, arrests, dismissals, or changes within the Nigerien armed forces could deepen internal divisions and disrupt command continuity and operational coordination. The replacement of armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salaou Barmou and other senior command changes following the August mutiny indicate ongoing restructuring, although their effect on military effectiveness remains unclear. Further changes affecting commanders or units deployed in conflict-affected western regions would increase the likelihood of reduced counterinsurgency capacity.

items.title: Diversion of security capacity towards regime protection
items.description: Increased deployment of Nigerien forces and allied security partners to protect strategic sites, monitor military personnel, or respond to further threats against the government could divert personnel, intelligence, logistical capacity, and other resources from counterinsurgency operations. The government's reliance on Russia's Africa Corps to suppress the August mutiny and previous reinforcement of the security apparatus in Niamey indicate heightened concern over threats to regime security.

items.title: Disruption or blockade of strategic supply routes by non-state armed groups.
items.description: JNIM or ISSP attacks, checkpoints, or blockades affecting major routes connecting Niamey with Tillabéri, Téra, Ouallam, Banibangou, or Dosso would indicate growing ability to isolate state positions and population centres, restrict military resupply and civilian movement, and constrain humanitarian access.
items.resolutionCriterion: the number of major routes connecting Niamey with Tillabéri, Téra, Ouallam, Banibangou, or Dosso affected by sustained JNIM or ISSP blockades or disruptions. The threshold is at least one strategic route experiencing sustained disruption that significantly restricts civilian movement, military resupply, or humanitarian access.

items.title: Israeli decision formalising further territorial expansion
items.description: The Israeli Security Cabinet or Ministry of Defense formally authorises a further advance of the "Yellow Line" or designates areas east of it as permanent military exclusion zones or closed military areas.

items.title: Breakdown of post-conflict governance negotiations
items.description: Public suspension or collapse of negotiations on Hamas disarmament and post-conflict governance, including the reversal of the 26 July 2026 cabinet decision permitting the initial deployment of the International Stabilisation Force.

items.title: Further increase in "Yellow Line" expansion activity
items.description: ACLED records "Yellow Line" expansion and associated military-movement events exceeding the June–July 2026 baseline of 22 events per month, indicating an acceleration of territorial consolidation.

items.title: Expansion of large-scale evacuation order
items.description: Israeli authorities issue new evacuation orders covering entire neighbourhoods adjacent to the "Yellow Line", including Zeitoun, At Tuffah, Shujaiyya, eastern Deir al Balah, or northern Rafah, signalling preparations for further military expansion.

items.title: Implementation of E1 tender awards before the elections
items.description: Progress of the E1 tenders, including any reversal of the Attorney General's postponement, before or after 27 October, could move the plan from approval towards physical implementation and make it more difficult for a future government to reverse.

items.title: Post-election government commitment
items.description: If the current government retains power and continues to support E1, it could accelerate planning approvals, infrastructure works, and construction.

items.title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
items.description: El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation. Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.

items.title: Cancellation of the December 2026 elections
items.description: With the 2018 peace process now dead, the December 2026 elections represented one of the few remaining frameworks for legitimate political transition — yet the prerequisites for a credible vote do not exist. The National Elections Commission remains unfunded, forces have not been unified, and active fighting makes campaigning impossible across large parts of the country. A further cancellation would likely be interpreted by opposition groups as a permanent consolidation of power by Kiir's government, deepening ethnic grievances and accelerating recruitment into armed factions
items.resolutionCriterion: 100% would be the election being formally cancelled leading to deepening conflict.

items.title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
items.description: Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis.

items.title: Entanglement with the war in Sudan
items.description: South Sudan's conflict risks becoming entangled with the war in Sudan. Though Juba has maintained official neutrality, its close links to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which control much of Sudan's border with South Sudan, are widely observed. The Sudanese army is suspected of reactivating ties with Nuer opposition forces in a bid to pressure Kiir and disrupt RSF supply lines — a dynamic that, if confirmed, would effectively transform Upper Nile into a proxy theatre of Sudan's war. Compounding this, Uganda's continued military backing of Kiir is not guaranteed; Kampala's willingness to underwrite his survival is uncertain given South Sudan's economic collapse and Uganda's competing regional commitments. A withdrawal of Ugandan support, combined with increasing Sudanese entanglement, could significantly alter the military balance, accelerating conflict escalation and further collapsing humanitarian access

items.title: RSF advances north from Baw
items.description: RSF movement towards Ed Damazine or the Roseires Dam corridor would indicate expansion beyond current front lines and increase displacement risk.

items.title: Expanded RSF-SPLM-N operational coordination
items.description: Visible coordination, redeployment, or logistics through SPLM-N/Al Hilu areas would suggest a more sustained offensive capacity.

items.title: Intercommunal mobilisation or retaliatory violence
items.description: Arming, inflammatory messaging, or clashes among communities affected by displacement and resource pressure would raise protection risks.

items.title: RSF encirclement of Al Obeid
items.description: Further RSF deployment west/south of Al Obeid, road interdiction, or attacks on access routes would indicate renewed siege formation.

items.title: Sustained drone or artillery attacks on Al Obeid
items.description: Repeated strikes on civilian, logistics, or service infrastructure would indicate escalation beyond localised insecurity.

items.title: Sharp decline in commercial or aid flows
items.description: Market shortages, fuel constraints, and reduced humanitarian access into Al Obeid would show siege conditions translating into humanitarian deterioration.

items.title: Extension or enforcement of goods bans
items.description: Renewed decrees, checkpoint enforcement, or seizures of goods moving towards RSF-controlled areas would tighten market supply.

items.title: Disruption of Al Na’am/Abyei market routes
items.description: Fire, insecurity, border tensions, or armed-party interference at Al Na’am would reduce alternative supply capacity.

items.title: Rapid price increases or market stock-outs
items.description: Sustained increases in food, fuel, medicine, or seed prices would indicate worsening market access and purchasing-power collapse.

items.title: SAF moves to integrate or restrict allied groups
items.description: Weapons restrictions, command integration orders, arrests, or removal of senior figures could provoke armed resistance.

items.title: Localised armed confrontations in Khartoum
items.description: Clashes around markets, garrisons, checkpoints, or strategic infrastructure would signal alliance fragmentation.

items.title: External pressure or sanctions increase
items.description: Additional sanctions or regional demands targeting SAF-linked Islamist groups could push SAF to act against allies.

items.title: Repeated drone attacks on Port Sudan or corridor infrastructure
items.description: Strikes on fuel depots, warehouses, port facilities, roads, or transport hubs would indicate escalation.

items.title: Expansion of RSF drone supply networks
items.description: Increased cargo flights, fighter camps, or weapons supply routes would raise RSF long-range strike capacity.

items.title: Disruption to fuel stocks or humanitarian dispatch
items.description: Fuel shortages, warehouse closures, or delayed convoy movements from Port Sudan would show operational impact.

items.title: Drone strikes directly hit Merowe Dam or grid infrastructure
items.description: Attacks on turbines, substations, transmission lines, or associated power facilities would increase outage risk.

items.title: Longer or more frequent power outages
items.description: Sustained blackouts in Khartoum, Port Sudan, Atbara, Dongola, or other dependent areas would indicate damage beyond temporary disruption.

items.title: Drone capability expansion through external supply
items.description: New long-range munitions, cross-border supply activity, or intensified RSF drone campaigns would raise the likelihood of damaging attacks.

items.title: Further aid cuts in eastern Chad
items.description: Reduced food, health, shelter, or cash assistance would increase pressure on refugees to return despite insecurity.

items.title: Expansion of refugee relocation from border areas
items.description: Broader relocation away from the Sudan border or fear linked to military deployment could prompt premature return decisions.

items.title: Increase in returns through West Darfur entry points
items.description: Rising IOM-recorded return movements or reports of households returning to contested areas would indicate materialisation.

items.title: Expansion of Israeli military control
items.description: A further expansion of Israeli positions, checkpoints or closed military zones beyond the current areas of control in Quneitra and western Dar'a could indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. If Israeli forces begin holding additional territory or restricting civilian access on a sustained basis, this could increase local resistance and create conditions for a broader Israeli-controlled zone extending towards areas linked to As-Sweida.

items.title: Renewed large-scale violence in As-Sweida
items.description: An escalation of violence between Druze groups, Syrian Government forces or other armed actors in As-Sweida could prompt Israel to reframe military intervention as necessary to protect the Druze population. This could revive calls for a Golan–As-Sweida humanitarian corridor and provide a justification for expanding or formalising Israeli military access in southern Syria.

items.title: Establishment of a settler outpost
items.description: Pioneers of Bashan or other Israeli settler groups successfully establishing a sustained civilian outpost inside southern Syria, rather than being detained and removed, could create pressure for Israeli forces to protect the settlement. This could accelerate the conversion of the existing military presence into a more permanent security or territorial arrangement.

items.title: Renewed Cross-Border Hostilities
items.description: Continued reciprocal attacks and restrictions on Sana’a Airport would reduce incentives for restraint and increase the risk of renewed cross-border hostilities.

items.title: Maritime escalation
items.description: Enforcement of the Houthi-declared maritime blockade or attacks on commercial shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait triggers broader international military involvement, including through the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition (announced 30 July 2026).

items.title: Large-Scale Intra-Yemeni Fighting
items.description: Intensified military mobilisation and sustained clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed IRG.

items.title: More refugees from South Sudan continue to arrive
Inability to cover gaps in response
Further Cuts in Food and Essential Services:
items.description: If humanitarian funding gaps persist through late 2025, food rations may fall below survival thresholds, while key services such as maternal health, water trucking, or protection casework may be scaled back or halted entirely. Such conditions could provoke unrest within camps or lead to unsafe self-relocation by refugees

items.title: Increase in New Arrivals Due to Regional Conflicts:
items.description: A spike in cross-border displacement particularly from Somalia’s Gedo region or Sudan’s Darfur could overwhelm current camp capacity. Without adequate contingency plans, the humanitarian system would be unable to absorb the new caseload, increasing protection risks, tension with host communities, and possible spillover of insecurity.

items.title: Increased crackdown on smuggling routes
items.description: The Syria–Lebanon border remains a major smuggling corridor for fuel, weapons, and drugs—particularly Captagon—facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. Efforts by Syria’s transitional Government to crack down on these routes have triggered violent resistance from local armed clans, risking further cross-border clashes in areas where smuggling underpins local power and livelihoods.

items.title: Hezbollah presence near the Lebanon - Syria border
items.description: Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeastern border, supported by allied Shia clans and control over key smuggling routes, is viewed by Syria’s transitional Government as a security threat. Although direct clashes have been avoided, rising tensions and recent incidents—including the shelling of Shia villages and weapons seizures—have strained relations between Hezbollah, Syria, and the Lebanese Government.

items.title: Violent demonstrations
items.description: The escalating protests, particularly the violent crackdown on the 3 June 2019 sit-in, can fuel further unrest and contribute to the instability of the transitional government.

items.title: Violence among armed groups
items.description: The internal divisions within the TMC and the RSF's involvement in violent actions, along with their historical role in conflicts such as in Darfur, contributes to the instability and fuel further violence.

items.title: Dbeibah’s consolidation of power in Tripoli
items.description: The recent defeat of rival factions (like Ghnewa) and Dbeibah’s expanding control could be perceived by the LNA as a threat or provocation, prompting a response.

items.title: Tripoli's perceived weakness
items.description: Saddam may see the internal reshuffling or instability in western Libya as an opportunity to reassert LNA influence.
